title: Knowledge Check 8: Lessons 57-64
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 57-64 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Accessibility guidance is organized around a small set of high-level principles rather than a flat symptom list. Which option is one of those principles?
options: Aesthetic
Adaptive
Scalable
Robust
questions.explanation: The four principles are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Every specific success criterion is an expression of one of them.

questions.question: A team builds a clickable div and layers ARIA roles onto it to mimic a button. Why is a native button element the better choice?
options: ARIA roles have been deprecated and must not be used on any element.
Native elements already provide keyboard and screen-reader behavior.
A native button automatically passes every top-tier criterion.
A div element cannot be styled, so the control would be invisible.
questions.explanation: Real semantic elements carry the keyboard handling and screen-reader semantics for free, so semantics come before ARIA. Layering roles onto a div works against the browser rather than with it.

questions.question: An automated accessibility scan passes with no findings. Why is that not proof the interface is accessible?
options: Scanners check only images and ignore every other element.
Scanners miss structural faults such as keyboard traps.
Scanners must be rerun after each new page is deployed.
Scanners fail whenever a base component is present.
questions.explanation: Scanners catch contrast and missing alt text but not structural problems such as a modal that traps focus or a screen-reader order that makes no sense. Those require manual keyboard and screen-reader passes.

questions.question: What separates a measurable non-functional requirement from one that only sounds like a requirement?
options: It names a quantity, a number, and the condition it applies under.
It is written last, after the whole detailed design section is complete.
It describes a feature the system must provide to end users.
It is approved by the executive sponsor long before the build.
questions.explanation: A measurable requirement names a quantity, a number, and a condition, as in a response-time target at a stated load. A phrase such as should be fast names none of them and cannot be verified.

questions.question: In a sequence diagram, how is a call that waits for a reply marked differently from one that does not wait?
options: A synchronous call uses a dotted line while a return call uses a solid one.
A synchronous call uses a solid arrowhead and an async signal a stick one.
Both call types use identical arrows and differ only in the frame label.
Synchronous calls sit above the lifelines and async calls below them.
questions.explanation: A synchronous call, where the sender waits, is drawn with a solid arrowhead, while an asynchronous signal uses a stick arrowhead. Return messages are optional and drawn as a dotted line with an open arrowhead.

questions.question: A solution must restore service within a stated time and tolerate only a stated amount of data loss. Which pair of recovery targets expresses that?
options: RPO for how long the solution can be down, and RTO for how much data loss is acceptable.
RTO and RPO both measure average response time under peak load.
RTO for how long the solution can be down and RPO for acceptable data loss.
SLA and SLO are the targets that define recovery time and data loss.
questions.explanation: RTO is how long the solution can be down and RPO is how much data the business accepts losing. Both together define how the solution behaves when something goes wrong and drive choices such as a replication or backup strategy.

questions.question: When presenting a design to a review board, what should the presenter do before stating the recommendation?
options: Limit the deck to the single recommended option to keep it short.
Present the alternatives weighed for each major choice and why each was rejected.
Name every stakeholder who supports the design so the board sees agreement.
List every platform feature in use so the board can gauge the design's technical depth.
questions.explanation: A strong presentation moves from the problem and constraints, to the alternatives weighed, to the recommendation and its reasoning. Naming the rejected alternatives shows the choice was reasoned rather than assumed.

questions.question: Why does a second review before deployment add value even after the design was already approved?
options: It re-approves the same design to create a formal paper trail for auditors.
It assigns blame when a deployment fails after the go-live date.
It confirms the built solution still matches the approved design.
It replaces the first review whenever the design changes during the build.
questions.explanation: Build drifts from design: a team swaps a pattern or wires data through a field nobody approved. The deploy-time review catches that drift while it is still the same project rather than a post-incident surprise.

questions.question: A board grants a temporary departure from a standing policy. What keeps it a controlled exception rather than a permanent gap?
options: Recording it with a named owner and a defined end date.
Approving it verbally so it does not clutter the policy documents.
Extending it each cycle automatically until the team requests a change.
Keeping it out of the project record so future teams are not confused.
questions.explanation: An exception exists to accommodate a temporary nonconformance while a better long-term fix is planned. Without an expiry and an owner it becomes a permanent hole in governance nobody remembers granting.

questions.question: A reviewer wants to judge whether an AI agent design will actually work. What should the presenter lead with?
options: A live demonstration of the agent answering several representative prompts.
An evaluation plan showing the evidence it works and where it is thin.
A single accuracy score computed on one curated dataset.
A list of platform features the design depends on.
questions.explanation: An AI system has no single behavior to demonstrate, only an expected behavior that is as trustworthy as the evaluation behind it. So the presenter leads with how the behavior was measured and where the evidence is weak.

questions.question: System logs mark an agent session as successful, yet reading the transcript shows the user never got their task done. What does this illustrate?
options: A P0 trust-breaking failure, because the agent gave a flatly wrong answer.
A benign artifact, because the log is the source of truth.
A phantom success, where the log reports a win the user did not get.
A model-layer regression, because the underlying model changed.
questions.explanation: This is a phantom success: telemetry reports a win that the user did not experience. It is why an AI review cannot stop at the logs and must count whether the user actually got what they needed.

questions.question: A board asks how the design prevents an agent from calling the wrong tool or endpoint. What is the strongest answer?
options: Show the written tool schemas, descriptions, and selection tests.
Rely on the model to choose the correct tool without added guidance.
Restrict the agent to a single tool so no wrong choice is possible.
Trust the outcome-layer evaluation, since final results confirm correctness.
questions.explanation: Tool selection depends on the contract between the model and each tool. Clear schemas and semantic descriptions, plus an evaluation that exercises selection under realistic inputs, are what keep the agent from invoking irrelevant tools.

questions.question: What credentials must a candidate hold before sitting for the CTA Review Board Exam?
options: The Application Architect and System Architect credentials.
A single current Salesforce Administrator certification.
Five signed client references and a portfolio review.
Any two Salesforce architect-track credentials of the candidate's choosing.
questions.explanation: Both the Application Architect and the System Architect credentials are hard prerequisites, covering what happens inside the org and between systems. The candidate must also pass the earlier evaluation stage before the board exam.

questions.question: The CTA design scenario is scored primarily on what, rather than on knowing any single pattern?
options: Reciting the correct integration pattern for every flow in the scenario.
Naming the largest possible number of platform features.
Integrating data, integration, identity, and governance coherently.
Finishing the written design faster than the other candidates.
questions.explanation: The exam is scored on the integration of concerns, not on individual expertise. The scenario asks for one coherent whole in which the data, integration, identity, and governance models stay consistent under a budget and a schedule.

questions.question: A candidate presents a polished design but cannot tie each component to a stated requirement. What is the core problem?
options: The design is far too detailed for the time the board allows in the session.
The candidate chose the wrong integration pattern for the flow.
The board scores a justification: each part must tie to a requirement.
The candidate failed to include a sequence diagram in the design.
questions.explanation: The board scores a justification, not a design. Every component should connect a requirement or constraint the client stated to a concrete architecture choice, and a part with no such link invites a judge's question.

questions.question: Before selecting any integration pattern for an enterprise, what decision must come first?
options: Which integration pattern the architect prefers for each flow.
Which middleware platform the client will license and operate.
Which system owns each fact, and which way it flows.
Which message format each connected system will emit.
questions.explanation: Ownership comes first because it sets the direction of flow and the failure semantics. Leaving ownership ambiguous creates two systems that both believe they are authoritative, which produces a reconciliation problem that cannot be designed away.

questions.question: A client has a few moderate, stable flows and a Salesforce-first team under a tight budget. Which reasoning about integration topology fits?
options: Salesforce as the hub fits moderate flows and a Salesforce-first team.
Middleware is always preferable because it centralizes every flow.
Point-to-point is always wrong because its links multiply faster than systems.
Topology should follow whichever pattern is currently fashionable.
questions.explanation: There is no universally correct topology. The honest call weighs the number and complexity of flows, the team's home platform, and the operating budget, then argues the fit rather than picking a favorite.

questions.question: Every new integration keeps reinterpreting the shared customer record differently across systems. Which standing decision contains that problem?
options: Force every system to rename its local fields to match the CRM.
Agree one canonical shape that every system maps to and from.
Move all enterprise data into one store so no mapping is needed.
Let each integration define its own mapping and document it apart.
questions.explanation: A canonical data model names one agreed representation for the objects that cross systems, and each system maps to and from it at its own boundary. This does not remove the differences; it contains them in one place so new integrations do not reinvent the mapping.

questions.question: Under the shared responsibility model, which controls does the customer design?
options: The physical data center, the network perimeter, and the platform.
Who may log in, what they may do, and how systems authenticate.
The provider's encryption services and its compliance certificates.
Nothing beyond choosing which cloud platform the company buys.
questions.explanation: The provider secures the cloud; the customer secures the org. That means defining who can log in, what they can do, how data is classified, and how integrations authenticate, rather than inheriting responsibility for controls never designed.

questions.question: A user can open a customer record but must not see the card number on it. Which access layer blocks the field?
options: The organization layer, through login IP ranges and hours.
The object layer, by removing read access to the whole object.
The field layer, through field-level security.
The record layer, by hiding the individual record.
questions.explanation: Field-level security controls whether a user can see and edit each individual field. Access is additive, and the most restrictive layer wins, so hiding the field blocks it regardless of object and record access.

questions.question: A regulated field must be encrypted but does not need to support filtering or sorting. Which encryption choice fits?
options: Deterministic Shield Platform Encryption, because it is the stronger scheme.
Volume-level encryption alone, with no field-level scheme added.
No encryption at rest, relying on encrypted transport instead.
Probabilistic Shield Platform Encryption, since filtering is not needed.
questions.explanation: Probabilistic encryption is the stronger default because identical values do not encrypt to identical ciphertext, and deterministic encryption is reserved for fields that must be filtered or sorted. Since exact-match filtering is not required here, probabilistic fits.

questions.question: Three systems hold the same customer and disagree. What is the first strategy decision that resolves it?
options: Name the one system that is authoritative for that domain.
Merge all copies and let the most recent write win.
Replicate every field into all three systems continuously.
Report the disagreement to the business and let each team decide.
questions.explanation: A single source of truth is a governance decision that names which system wins when two disagree. Without it, every report reconciles the systems by hand and nobody can say which version is correct.

questions.question: Multiple records describe the same real-world customer. What does linking them into one profile actually do?
options: It selects a winning value and overwrites the source records.
It creates a golden record that replaces all the originals.
It links records for a use without overwriting sources.
It guarantees every linked field is complete and accurate.
questions.explanation: Identity resolution links records so the right source value can be chosen for a given use; it is not a golden record and does not overwrite source data. Treating unify-as-overwrite destroys the traceability that governance and lineage depend on.

questions.question: A dashboard figure is disputed. What makes lineage the authoritative answer?
options: It reruns the report until the very same number is reproduced again.
It records the data's origin and every transformation applied.
It stores a snapshot of the raw layer for each report.
It names the engineer who originally built the dashboard.
questions.explanation: Lineage is the traceable record of where data originated and every transformation it passed through. It must span from the source system to the consuming report, because any untraceable hop breaks the chain and turns the answer into a guess.
